outline.h2: What is SaaS homepage design, and what is the homepage for?
outline.answerHint: **SaaS homepage design is the design of the first page of your marketing site, and its job is to make one promise clearly enough that the right visitor signs up expecting exactly what the product shows next.** (≤35 words)
points: Definition from eav[0], then the twist: the homepage is the first screen of onboarding, not a brochure. Value perception happens before sign-up (Ramli John, eav[7]); realization happens in the product.
NN/g's core job (eav[1]): say what the company does and what users can accomplish. Expand Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) on first use.

One sentence on the difference from a campaign landing page: a landing page serves one ad or audience; the homepage serves every visitor type, so it carries navigation and several paths. Keep it to one or two sentences (landing page is a separate future topic).

First UP link to the hub inside the first 300 words: as a SaaS design agency team, we design the homepage, pricing page and sign-up together (hub FAQ). Anchor: 'SaaS design agency' or 'our SaaS product design team' (vary from the closing).
Bridge: 'Everything on the page depends on one sentence: the promise.'

outline.h2: What promise should a SaaS homepage make?
outline.answerHint: **A SaaS homepage should promise one result, for one kind of customer, that a new user can see inside the first session.**
points: Promise formula as a short visual or inline line: who it is for + the job + the result you can see. NN/g tagline guidance (eav[2]): brief, direct, no jargon.

Perceived vs experienced value (eav[6], Wes Bush via Productboard): every word in the headline sets an expectation the first run must meet. A bigger promise raises sign-ups and lowers activation if the product cannot show it fast.

Three illustrative weak → specific rewrites for HYPOTHETICAL US products (e.g., a scheduling tool for dental offices, a revenue analytics tool, an AI meeting-notes app). Label them hypothetical. Do not quote a real company's headline as weak.
The test I use (first person): can a new user see this result before they close the first tab? If not, the headline promises the roadmap, not the product.
Bridge: 'A promise needs evidence, and the rest of the page is that evidence, in a set order.'

outline.h2: Which sections does a SaaS homepage need, and in what order?
outline.answerHint: **Most SaaS homepages need 9 to 10 sections, ordered so the first screen carries the promise and the CTA, and every section below answers the next doubt a buyer has.**
points: Attention data: NN/g 57% of viewing time on the first screenful, 74% on the first two (eav[3]). So the hero carries headline, subheadline, primary CTA and a real product screen; nothing important sits only at the bottom.

Section table (visual + astext): hero; proof strip (logos with a named result where possible); how it works in 3 steps that mirror the real first-run steps; product screens by job or role; outcomes; integrations; security and compliance (SOC 2 report if you have one; HIPAA only for health data); pricing teaser or link; FAQ; final CTA. Column 3: what each must match in the product.
Length: no pixel rule (the '3,000–5,000 px' figure in the SERP is unsourced). Length follows the number of doubts the buyer has: a $20/month tool needs fewer sections than a $50,000/year platform.
Real product UI beats abstract illustration, because the screenshot is a preview of the first run. Keep screenshots current with the shipped product.
Bridge: 'The section that decides whether any of this pays off is the button.'

outline.h2: Should the homepage CTA offer a free trial, freemium or a demo?
outline.answerHint: **Choose the homepage CTA by how your product is sold: a free trial or freemium plan when users can reach value alone, a demo when setup or price needs a person, and both when buyers and users differ.**
points: Decision tree visual (visuals[2]) with astext: self-serve setup under one session → free trial or freemium; setup needs data migration, integrations or security review → book a demo; mixed → primary trial + secondary demo.
CTA label: NN/g 'Get Started' finding (eav[5], 6 of 8 participants). Write labels that say what happens next ('Start a free trial', 'See a 20-minute demo', illustrative). One primary CTA per screen.

Card or no card: if the trial takes a card and turns paid, ROSCA applies (eav[15]): disclose material terms before billing details, get express consent, offer simple cancellation. Note the click-to-cancel rule was vacated on July 8, 2025, but ROSCA and state auto-renewal laws still apply. One line: not legal advice; ask your counsel. 'No credit card required' appears only if true.

Pricing on the homepage: a teaser or a clear link to the pricing page when plans are public; NN/g says an unclear business model makes users suspicious (eav[1] source page). Do not design the pricing page here (future post).
Bridge: 'Whatever the button says, the next screen has to agree with it.'

outline.h2: How do you make the homepage promise match the first minutes in the product?
outline.answerHint: **Map every homepage claim to the screen where a new user experiences it, keep the sign-up form short, and make the first screen after sign-up start the exact job the headline promised.**
points: THE CORE SERP GAP. Flow map visual (visuals[3]): headline → CTA → sign-up form → first screen → first result, with the promise as a thread.

Sign-up form: NN/g minimum fields, Google/Microsoft sign-in, no confirm fields (eav[8]). Echo the homepage promise on the sign-up page so the visitor knows they are on the same path. Name the hub deliverable: account creation, workspace setup, invites and a checklist (eav[16]).

First screen: if the promise is a report, the first screen offers sample data or one import step toward that report, not a blank dashboard. NN/g empty states: show status, teach in context, link to the step (eav[9]).

Cross-hub link (the post's ONE): when the gap sits in sign-up, setup and empty states, that is SaaS onboarding design work → /services/saas-products/saas-onboarding-design/. Do not explain onboarding patterns, checklists or tours here (that hub and its posts own them).

Lead asset: the promise ledger (visuals[4] + astext with 3 illustrative rows). Columns: homepage claim | screen where the user sees it | minutes from sign-up | kept / missing | fix in copy or in product.

DOWN link: Digno (eav[19]): we delivered the website and the web app together; the homepage explains how Digno works and invites visitors to try it free. Describe only what the case study says; no results attributed to the homepage.
LEAD ANGLE lives here (see leadAngle). End with one natural invitation in the 'we' voice from the hub FAQ.

outline.h2: How does a B2B SaaS homepage serve buyers and users at once?
outline.answerHint: **A B2B SaaS homepage serves two readers: the user who wants to see the job done and the buyer who needs proof, security and price, so it gives each a path without splitting the promise.**
points: Hyponym H2 (B2B SaaS homepage). Roles: end user, admin, economic buyer, security reviewer. Use-case or role tabs as one pattern; one promise above them.
Trust for buyers: named results over anonymous logo walls; a security page with the SOC 2 report status; integrations they already run. Do not claim compliance the reader's product lacks.
Demo path: what the demo page asks (fields that route the lead, not 12 questions), and that the demo shows the same first-run screens the homepage pictures.
Admin vs invited member is an onboarding topic; one sentence only, no link to other-silo posts.
Bridge: 'The homepage is one page of several, and they have to read as one product.'

outline.h2: What does web design for SaaS need beyond the homepage?
outline.answerHint: **Web design for SaaS needs a small set of pages that carry the homepage promise forward: pricing, product or feature pages, use cases, integrations, security, sign-up and the first screen in the app.**
points: Carry the secondary keyword here (see keywordCarrier).
Page set as a short list with each page's job. The pricing page gets one sentence (plans, limits, upgrade path) and no deep design advice (future post 'saas pricing page design').

Consistency: one design system across site and product, so the screenshot on the homepage, the sign-up page and the first app screen use the same components and type. Tie to the hub deliverable 'Design system' (Figma library with tokens that match front-end code).
Pillar mention once: /services/saas-products/ (SaaS product design) for teams that need the site and product designed as one system.
Bridge: 'Once the pages exist, test the path, not just the page.'

outline.h2: How do you test a SaaS homepage before and after launch?
outline.answerHint: **Test a SaaS homepage in two stages: before launch, check that people understand the promise and find the CTA; after launch, judge the page by what its sign-ups do in the product.**
points: Before launch: five-second test (what does this company do, for whom?), first-click test on the CTA, a short moderated session that continues through sign-up into the first screen. Lindgaard (eav[4]) only as context that visual judgments form fast; state its limit (visual appeal only).

Metrics table (visuals[5] + astext): visit → sign-up start (CTA click rate), sign-up start → complete (form completion), sign-up → first result (activation rate of homepage sign-ups, time to first value), trial → paid. Hub metrics (eav[18]).
Benchmark with the right label: Unbounce 2024 median SaaS landing page conversion 3.8% (eav[10]); it is a landing-page figure, so compare trends in your own data, not your homepage against it.

Technical gates, US frame: LCP ≤ 2.5 s and INP ≤ 200 ms (eav[11]); heavy autoplay hero video is the usual LCP problem. WCAG 2.2 AA with ADA/Section 508 as the US frame: contrast 4.5:1 over screenshots (eav[12]), 24 px targets (eav[13]), cookie banner must not hide the focused CTA (eav[14]).

Session recordings and heatmaps after launch (Microsoft Clarity is in our tool list in content/home.ts). A/B test one element at a time once traffic allows; low-traffic B2B sites rely on qualitative tests.
Bridge: 'Most failed tests trace back to a handful of mistakes.'

outline.h2: Which SaaS homepage design mistakes break the promise?
outline.answerHint: **The costliest SaaS homepage design mistakes are the ones that make a promise the first session can't keep: a vague headline, a generic CTA, stock art instead of the product, and a sign-up that asks too much.**
points: Reasoned list, situation + because (not a numbered audit, which the onboarding silo used): vague category headline; 'Get Started' with no destination; abstract illustration or outdated screenshot; claims tied to roadmap features; three equal CTAs; logo wall with no named result; heavy hero video failing LCP; cookie banner covering the CTA; sign-up form with job title, company size and phone before value; first screen is a blank dashboard.
Each item names its fix in one clause and which part it belongs to (copy, page, sign-up, product). Items in the product column lead back to the hub service.

Second invitation (optional, short): we run the homepage, sign-up and first screen as one design project; describe only hub facts (6 to 16 weeks for full products, metrics agreed at kick-off). Do NOT quote a homepage-only price (the hub publishes none).
Bridge to Bottom line.

outline.answerHint: 2–4 sentences, before the FAQs. Not counted in the content H2s.
points: Restate the idea: write the promise the first session keeps, order the page around buyer doubts, and judge it by what sign-ups do next.
The author's recommendation in one first-person sentence with NO label ('My recommendation:' is used in saas-onboarding).
CTA (MOFU: case study + consultation): fill in the promise ledger; for every claim marked 'missing', book a free consultation. Second UP link to the hub (deep link to the FAQ section, varied anchor).

faqs.q: Is a SaaS homepage the same as a landing page?
faqs.a: No. A landing page serves one campaign or audience with one CTA. A SaaS homepage serves every visitor type, so it carries navigation, several paths and the company's main promise.

faqs.q: Should a SaaS homepage show pricing?
faqs.a: Yes, when your plans are public: a short teaser or a clear link to the pricing page. NN/g notes that an unclear business model makes visitors suspicious. Sales-led products can link to a pricing overview and a demo instead.

faqs.q: How long should a SaaS homepage be?
faqs.a: As long as the buyer's doubts. A low-priced self-serve tool needs fewer sections than an enterprise platform. Keep the promise, the CTA and a real product screen on the first screen, where NN/g found 57% of viewing time goes.

faqs.q: Can we use a template for our SaaS homepage?
faqs.a: Yes, for layout. A template cannot write your promise or design your sign-up and first screen, and those decide whether homepage visitors activate.

faqs.q: How do you measure SaaS homepage success?
faqs.a: By what homepage visitors do next: CTA click rate, sign-up completion, activation rate of homepage sign-ups and time to first value, compared before and after the redesign.

visuals.idea: Five frames left to right: homepage hero (headline + CTA) → sign-up form (email, Google sign-in) → first screen (sample data, one highlighted action) → first result (the report or outcome the headline promised). A single colored 'promise' thread runs through the headline, the sign-up page echo and the first result. Text panel: the five steps with what each must say or show.

A tall homepage wireframe with the 9–10 sections stacked, each tagged with its job ('promise', 'proof', 'how it works = first-run steps', 'security', 'pricing teaser'), and a side band showing NN/g's 57% (first screen) and 17% (second screen) attention split. Text panel: the section table.

Start: 'Can a new user reach value alone in one session?' Branches by setup effort and price to: free trial (no card), free trial with card (ROSCA disclosure flag), freemium, book a demo, trial + demo. Must not look like the zigzag tree of design-system-roi or the mobile post's tree: use a horizontal tree with pill-shaped endpoints. Text panel: the routes as a list.

The promise ledger as a ledger-book page: columns claim | screen where the user sees it | minutes from sign-up | kept / missing | fix in copy or product. 3 illustrative rows for a hypothetical analytics SaaS (one marked 'missing' in red), 3 blank. Not the rule-sheet look of user-onboarding-automation: use ledger ruling and a stamp for 'kept'. Text panel: columns and the 3 rows.

Three side-by-side hero cards for hypothetical US products: vague headline + 'Get Started' (before) vs specific promise + labeled CTA (after), each with a one-line note on what the first screen must then show. Text panel: the three pairs.

Four stages (visit → sign-up start → sign-up complete → first result) as a funnel with the metric at each step and the test that diagnoses each drop (five-second test, first-click test, session recordings, A/B test). No numbers presented as benchmarks. Text panel: the metrics table.

leadAngle: The moment: H2 5. The reader fills in the promise ledger and finds homepage claims with no screen in the first session, or a first screen that starts somewhere else. Copy can be fixed alone; a missing first-run path cannot. Offer, in hub facts only: we design the marketing site, pricing page and sign-up flow together so the promise on the website matches the first minutes in the product (hub FAQ), measured by 2 or 3 metrics agreed at kick-off (activation rate, time to first value, trial-to-paid conversion). DOWN proof: Digno (website + web app). Closing: 'For every claim marked missing, book a free consultation.' Do not promise a free audit, a homepage-only price, a reply time other than the site standard (within one business day, ET), or development work.

CASE STUDIES: Digno is the only case study whose scope lists the website AND shows the homepage (lines 29, 91, 93): use it as the DOWN link, describing only the homepage headline, the 'How Digno works' block and the try-free invitation. Do not attribute Digno's 126% / 5x / 13:1 / 50% results to the homepage. Elia Wellness, Nitro and Anyday also list 'website' in scope, but only Nitro describes it (an NFT game site, off-audience). TradeZella shows a website image but its scope does not list the website: do not claim we designed it.

EXAMPLES: use HYPOTHETICAL US products for headline rewrites and the ledger (label them). Do not critique a real company's homepage, and do not describe a real SaaS homepage's current content (homepages change; facts must be verifiable on publish day). Digno is the only real homepage named.

DO NOT USE (unsourced, seen in the SERP): 'a SaaS homepage has 3 seconds to convince visitors'; '3,000 to 5,000 pixels' page length; 'one or two strong proof signals beat many weak ones' as a measured finding (tenet's 28-site study is a design review, not a conversion test; may be mentioned only as 'fewer than half of 28 SaaS homepages Tenet reviewed put social proof in the hero' if the fact-checker confirms the page); Dribbble/agency homepage prices ($400, $1,500, $2,900–$10,000, '$18k'); 'busy homepages slow load times' with no data; Unbounce's older 2.9% / 24.2% SaaS figures (undated); Tractinsky '10 ms'.

FACT-CHECKER FLAGS: (1) NN/g get-started: confirm '6 of 8' and the meal-delivery context. (2) NN/g homepage-design-principles: confirm the tagline and business-model wording. (3) Ramli John: 'moment of value perception before sign-up' confirmed only via a reader summary. (4) Unbounce 3.8% / 6.6%: confirm year 2024 on the page. (5) ROSCA: confirm the three requirements on the FTC page and that no replacement negative-option rule took effect after July 8, 2025. (6) Lindgaard: state only the visual-appeal finding.

ABBREVIATIONS to expand on first use: software as a service (SaaS), call to action (CTA), Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g), Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), Federal Trade Commission (FTC), System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2), single sign-on (SSO), user experience (UX).

'We' only for hub facts (marketing site + pricing page + sign-up designed together; metrics at kick-off; design system deliverable) and the Digno case study. No invented anecdotes or clients.
